newsitem.title: USA: NBA BASKETBALL-RODMAN FINED RECORD $50,000 BUT NOT SUSPENDED.
newsitem.headline: NBA BASKETBALL-RODMAN FINED RECORD $50,000 BUT NOT SUSPENDED.

text.p: NBA Commissioner David Stern fined Dennis Rodman $50,000 Thursday but did not suspend the Chicago Bulls bad boy for obscenity-laced comments he made about Mormons during the league's championship series.
"I have indicated in previous actions that insensitive or derogatory comments involving race or other classifications are unacceptable in the NBA," Stern said in a statement.
"Dennis Rodman's comments were exactly the kind of offensive remarks that cannot be tolerated or excused," Stern said.

The fine doubles the previous largest NBA fine of $25,000, levied three times, but the league did not go so far as to suspend the six-time NBA rebounding champion, who will be available to play for Chicago in Game 6 of the Finals Friday.
The defending champion Bulls stand one win away from their fifth championship, leading the Utah Jazz three games to two in the best-of-seven Finals.
Rodman, in a bizarre explanation of his poor play in the Finals, said last Saturday that he could not get his game in sync because of all the "asshole Mormons" in Utah.

Rodman -- who on Tuesday made a clumsy attempt to explain his remarks by saying "The Mormons don't like me either, right?" and claiming he was a frequent target of abuse in Utah -- apologised at the Bulls' practice facility here Thursday.
"As far as religion, it's not about trying to put down anybody's religion," Rodman said. "I apologise for that."
But he rapped the NBA's action: "They have no reason, no business to even get involved. Like I said, I apologise for the religion."
Bulls coach Phil Jackson believes Rodman did not intend to disparage the Mormon religion.

"To Dennis, a Mormon may be just a nickname for people from Utah," said Jackson. "He may not even know it's a religious cult or sect, or whatever it is. I don't know what Dennis even associates with it."
The Mormon church -- The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, whose members make up about 70 percent of the Utah population -- declined comment on the controversy.
But anti-bigotry groups condemned Rodman's comments.

During the week that the NBA Finals were in Salt Lake City -- for Games 3, 4 and 5 -- Rodman fled strait-laced Utah to relax in anything-goes Las Vegas in neighbouring Nevada for two nights in a row, saying he "wanted to get the hell out of here and relax."

Rodman's unusual lifestyle choices -- which include ever-changing garish hair colours, cross-dressing, body-piercing and gambling -- are the polar opposite of Mormon beliefs, which do not allow smoking, swearing or the consumption of alcohol or caffeine.
The most recent $25,000 fine was against New Jersey Nets coach John Calipari earlier this season for calling a sportswriter a "stupid Mexican."
Rodman this season drew three suspensions that cost him 14 games and more than $1.2 million in fines and lost salary.
He was suspended for a pair of games by the Bulls in December for swearing during a live postgame interview.
He also drew a one-game ban from the league for a tussle with Milwaukee Bucks forward Joe Wolf in March.
The biggest suspension was an 11-game ban for kicking a courtside cameraman during a game at Minnesota on January 15.

Rodman, who also drew a $25,000 fine for the cameraman incident, has continued his temperamental play in the postseason. After averaging 16.1 rebounds per contest during the season, he has managed just 8.3 per game in the playoffs while collecting a record 17 technical fouls in 18 games.
Rodman earned $9 million this season and becomes a free agent on July 1. Speculation is strong that Rodman has worn out his welcome with the Bulls and will not be re-signed.
